title: How to Put Your Existing API in Claude, Teams and WhatsApp in Under 15 Minutes
excerpt: Your application already does the work. Here's how to make it usable from Claude, Microsoft Teams and WhatsApp — no MCP server or bot to write — with every action taken as the person who asked.
contentHtml:
Your software has an API. It can create a ticket, pull an invoice, list today's jobs. But your users spend their day in Teams, on WhatsApp or in Claude. Between the two, there's no bridge.

Building that bridge yourself means writing an MCP server, handling OAuth for every user, storing your application's credentials somewhere the AI can't read them, logging every call — then doing it all again for Teams and for WhatsApp. Weeks of work.

This guide shows the short version with api0: import the API once, choose who can sign in, and connect the channels.

What you need

  • An HTTP API reachable from the internet (REST/JSON).
  • Its description: an OpenAPI spec (YAML or JSON), or failing that, the list of your endpoints.
  • A Google account to sign in to app.api0.ai.
  • For Teams: access to the Azure portal. For WhatsApp: a Meta Business account.

No API at hand to try it? Take one of the sample specs (CRM, ticketing, invoicing, field service, HR) and point it at a mock server.

Step 1 — Import the API (3 minutes)

  1. Sign in at app.api0.ai.
  2. Tools tab → import your OpenAPI spec.
  3. Each operation becomes a tool: its name, description and parameters are what Claude sees.
  4. A built-in test calls each tool before it counts as configured.

No spec? Describe your endpoints in plain English and api0 turns them into tools.

The tip that changes everything: write good descriptions. Claude picks a tool from its description. Say when to use it ("use before creating a contact, to avoid duplicates") and what to confirm before an irreversible action ("ask for confirmation before sending an invoice"). A good description is worth ten lines of prompt.

A few details handled for you:

  • parameter names MCP clients reject ($filter, page[size]) are exposed under a clean name (filter, page_size) and sent to your API under their real name;
  • an error from your application comes back to Claude as a readable result, so it can correct and retry;
  • a failed call is never billed.

Step 2 — Set up access (3 minutes)

Access tab. Two questions.

Who can sign in? By default, people sign in with Google. A company can plug in its own identity provider (Entra ID or any OIDC provider): its employees then sign in with their usual account.

Which credential is your application called with? This is the key question. The options, simplest to finest:

Option For
Identity token signed by api0 Your own application: it verifies the call comes from api0 and for which tenant. No secret to store.
Fixed token or headers A third-party API with a single key.
OAuth client credentials An API that issues service tokens.
Each person's own credential Each user adds their own token, or connects their account via OAuth: every action is taken as them, with their permissions.

In every case, the credential stays in api0. Claude never sees it.

A third setting: who pays for paid tools — the tenant, or each person on their own plan.

Step 3 — Claude (2 minutes)

Channels tab → MCP. You'll find your tenant's MCP server URL and a Client ID.

In claude.ai → Settings → Connectors → Add custom connector:

  1. paste the server URL;
  2. choose "Use your own OAuth client" and paste the Client ID (not the URL), with no secret;
  3. sign in.

That's it. Ask Claude "what tools do you have?", then ask a real question. For a team, create a Claude Project with domain instructions (a template is provided).

Cursor, Claude Desktop and other MCP clients connect the same way.

Step 4 — Teams (5 minutes, on the Azure side)

Microsoft doesn't let a third party set up a bot for you: you need an Azure Bot resource in your name. api0 does the rest.

  1. Azure portal → create an Azure Bot → note the App ID, create a secret.
  2. app.api0.ai → Channels → Teams: paste the App ID, secret and tenant ID. api0 checks with Microsoft that they work and gives you the messaging endpoint.
  3. Paste that endpoint into the Azure bot's configuration and enable the Teams channel.
  4. Download the Teams app package api0 generates (manifest and icons) and install it.

The full walkthrough is in Put Your Product in Teams Without Building a Bot.

Step 5 — WhatsApp or Telegram (2 minutes)

Telegram: create a bot with @BotFather and paste the token into Channels → Telegram. api0 checks the token and sets up the webhook itself.

WhatsApp: in Channels → WhatsApp, enter the Phone Number ID, a permanent token and a verify token of your choice. Then paste the Webhook URL api0 gives you into your Meta app's WhatsApp configuration and subscribe to messages.

Either way, you can give the bot a system prompt (short answers, confirm before acting…). On their first message, each person links their account once; after that they talk to your API like a colleague.

What you get

  • One setup for Claude, Teams, WhatsApp and Telegram: the same tools everywhere.
  • Every action taken as the person, with their permissions in your system.
  • No secrets in the AI: credentials stay encrypted in api0.
  • A log of every call (Activity tab) and credits per call.
  • Nothing to host: no MCP server, no bot, no new interface.

FAQ

My API is private, behind a VPN. api0 needs to reach it. Put it behind a gateway that only accepts calls signed by api0 (the "signed identity token" option).

I want to limit what the AI can do. Import only the operations that are useful, and prefer each person's own credential: your application then applies its own permissions.

title: Comment mettre ton API existante dans Claude, Teams et WhatsApp en moins de 15 minutes
excerpt: Ton application fait déjà le travail. Voici comment la rendre utilisable depuis Claude, Microsoft Teams et WhatsApp, sans écrire de serveur MCP ni de bot, avec chaque action faite au nom de la personne qui demande.
contentHtml:
Ton logiciel a une API. Elle sait créer un ticket, sortir une facture, lister les interventions du jour. Mais tes utilisateurs, eux, passent leur journée dans Teams, sur WhatsApp ou dans Claude. Entre les deux, il manque un pont.

Construire ce pont soi-même, c'est écrire un serveur MCP, gérer l'OAuth pour chaque utilisateur, stocker les identifiants de ton application quelque part où l'IA ne peut pas les lire, journaliser chaque appel, puis recommencer pour Teams et pour WhatsApp. Des semaines de travail.

Ce guide montre la version courte avec api0 : on importe l'API une fois, on choisit qui peut se connecter, et on branche les canaux.

Ce qu'il te faut

  • Une API HTTP accessible depuis Internet (REST/JSON).
  • Sa description : une spec OpenAPI (YAML ou JSON), ou à défaut la liste de tes endpoints.
  • Un compte Google pour te connecter à app.api0.ai.
  • Pour Teams : un accès au portail Azure. Pour WhatsApp : un compte Meta Business.

Pas d'API sous la main pour essayer ? Prends une des specs d'exemple (CRM, tickets, facturation, interventions, RH) et pointe-la vers un serveur de mock.

Étape 1 — Importer l'API (3 minutes)

  1. Connecte-toi sur app.api0.ai.
  2. Onglet Tools → importe ta spec OpenAPI.
  3. Chaque opération devient un outil : son nom, sa description et ses paramètres sont ce que Claude verra.
  4. Un test intégré appelle chaque outil avant qu'il soit compté comme configuré.

Pas de spec ? Tu peux décrire tes endpoints en langage naturel, api0 les transforme en outils.

Le conseil qui change tout : soigne les descriptions. Claude choisit un outil d'après sa description. Écris quand l'utiliser (« à utiliser avant de créer un contact, pour éviter les doublons ») et quoi confirmer avant une action irréversible (« demande confirmation avant d'envoyer une facture »). Une bonne description vaut plus que dix lignes de prompt.

Quelques détails gérés pour toi :

  • les paramètres aux noms que les clients MCP refusent ($filter, page[size]) sont exposés sous un nom propre (filter, page_size) et renvoyés à ton API sous leur vrai nom ;
  • une erreur de ton application revient à Claude comme un résultat lisible, pour qu'il puisse corriger et réessayer ;
  • un appel qui échoue n'est jamais facturé.

Étape 2 — Régler l'accès (3 minutes)

Onglet Access. Deux questions.

Qui peut se connecter ? Par défaut, les gens se connectent avec Google. Une entreprise peut brancher son propre fournisseur d'identité (Entra ID ou tout fournisseur OIDC) : ses employés se connectent alors avec leur compte habituel.

Avec quel identifiant ton application est-elle appelée ? C'est la question clé. Les options, de la plus simple à la plus fine :

Option Pour qui
Jeton d'identité signé par api0 Ta propre application : elle vérifie que l'appel vient d'api0 et pour quel tenant. Aucun secret à stocker.
Jeton ou en-têtes fixes Une API tierce avec une clé unique.
OAuth client credentials Une API qui délivre des jetons de service.
Identifiant de chaque personne Chaque utilisateur ajoute son propre jeton, ou connecte son compte en OAuth : chaque action est faite en son nom, avec ses droits.

Dans tous les cas, l'identifiant reste dans api0. Claude ne le voit jamais.

Troisième réglage : qui paie les outils payants, le tenant ou chaque personne avec son propre plan.

Étape 3 — Claude (2 minutes)

Onglet Channels → MCP. Tu y trouves l'URL du serveur MCP de ton tenant et un Client ID.

Dans claude.ai → Paramètres → Connecteurs → Ajouter un connecteur personnalisé :

  1. colle l'URL du serveur ;
  2. choisis « Use your own OAuth client » et colle le Client ID (pas l'URL), sans secret ;
  3. connecte-toi.

C'est tout. Demande à Claude « quels outils as-tu ? », puis pose une vraie question. Pour une équipe, crée un Projet Claude avec des instructions métier (un template est fourni).

Cursor, Claude Desktop et les autres clients MCP se connectent de la même façon.

Étape 4 — Teams (5 minutes, côté Azure)

Microsoft ne laisse pas un service tiers configurer un bot à ta place : il faut une ressource Azure Bot à ton nom. api0 fait tout le reste.

  1. Portail Azure → crée un Azure Bot → note l'App ID, crée un secret.
  2. app.api0.ai → Channels → Teams : colle App ID, secret et ID de tenant. api0 vérifie auprès de Microsoft qu'ils fonctionnent et te donne le messaging endpoint.
  3. Colle cet endpoint dans la configuration du bot Azure, active le canal Teams.
  4. Télécharge le package d'app Teams généré par api0 (manifest et icônes) et installe-le.

Le détail pas à pas est dans le guide Mettre ton produit dans Teams sans développer de bot.

Étape 5 — WhatsApp ou Telegram (2 minutes)

Telegram : crée un bot avec @BotFather, colle le token dans Channels → Telegram. api0 vérifie le token et branche le webhook lui-même.

WhatsApp : dans Channels → WhatsApp, renseigne le Phone Number ID, un token permanent et un verify token de ton choix. Colle ensuite la Webhook URL fournie par api0 dans la configuration WhatsApp de ton app Meta et abonne-toi aux messages.

Dans les deux cas, tu peux donner au bot un prompt système (réponses courtes, confirmation avant les actions…). Au premier message, chaque personne relie son compte une fois ; ensuite elle parle à ton API comme à un collègue.

Ce que tu obtiens

  • Une seule configuration pour Claude, Teams, WhatsApp et Telegram : les mêmes outils partout.
  • Chaque action au nom de la personne, avec ses droits dans ton système.
  • Aucun secret dans l'IA : les identifiants restent chiffrés dans api0.
  • Un journal de chaque appel (onglet Activity) et des crédits par appel.
  • Rien à héberger : pas de serveur MCP, pas de bot, pas de nouvelle interface.

Questions fréquentes

Mon API est privée, derrière un VPN. api0 doit pouvoir l'atteindre. Expose-la derrière une passerelle qui n'accepte que les appels signés par api0 (option « jeton d'identité signé »).

Je veux limiter ce que l'IA peut faire. N'importe que les opérations utiles, et préfère l'identifiant de chaque personne : ton application applique alors ses propres droits.

title: Put Your Product in Teams Without Building a Bot
excerpt: Your customers live in Microsoft Teams. Here's how to put your product there — in conversation, with each user's own permissions — without writing, hosting or maintaining a bot.
contentHtml:
When a B2B customer asks "do you have anything in Teams?", the honest answer is often no. Because a Teams bot is not a small project:

  • an Azure Bot resource, an app registration, secrets that expire;
  • a web service that receives Bot Framework messages and replies;
  • a conversation engine that understands requests and calls your API;
  • per-user authentication, so each person acts only with their own permissions;
  • a Teams app manifest, icons, approval by the customer's admin;
  • and maintenance for all of it.

With api0, you keep the one part Microsoft requires — the Azure Bot resource — and the rest is provided.

How it works

Teams user ──► Azure Bot (yours) ──► api0 ──► your API
                                      │
                         tools, identity, log, credits
  1. The user messages the bot in a private Teams chat.
  2. Microsoft forwards the message to the messaging endpoint api0 provides.
  3. api0's assistant understands the request and calls the tools built from your API — as that user.
  4. The answer comes back in Teams.

These are the same tools as in Claude or WhatsApp: you set up your API once.

Before you start

  • Your API imported into api0 (Tools tab) — see the main guide.
  • Access set up (Access tab): ideally each person's own credential, so your application applies their permissions.
  • Access to the Azure portal with the right to create an Azure Bot resource.
  • On the customer side: a Teams admin who approves the app, or custom app upload allowed.

Step 1 — Create the Azure Bot resource

  1. Azure portal → Create a resource → Azure Bot.
  2. Bot name, subscription, resource group. Pricing tier: F0.
  3. App type: Single Tenant. Note the App ID (a GUID) and the Microsoft tenant ID.
  4. In the resource → Configuration → Manage Password → New client secret. Copy the value right away: Azure only shows it once.

Step 2 — Register it in api0

app.api0.ai → Channels → Teams:

  • App ID, secret, Microsoft tenant ID;
  • bot name (the one your users will see);
  • optional: a system prompt (tone, answer length, confirmations).

api0 immediately asks Microsoft for a token with these values. If the App ID and secret don't belong together, you know right away, with a clear message — not three days later in production.

In return, api0 shows your bot's messaging endpoint.

Step 3 — Point Azure at api0

In the Azure Bot resource:

  1. Configuration → Messaging endpoint → paste the URL from api0 → Apply.
  2. Channels → Microsoft Teams → accept the terms → Apply.

Step 4 — The Teams app package

A bot reaches nobody until a Teams app naming it is installed. That app is a zip: a manifest.json and two icons. This is often where projects stall.

In Channels → Teams, api0 generates the package from what it already knows: App ID, bot name, your tenant's Get started page. You download it, and that's it.

The app is personal scope: the bot answers in one-to-one chats, where it makes sense.

Prefer to build it yourself (branded icons, your own text)? A manifest template is provided.

Step 5 — Install and test

  • For yourself: Teams → Apps → Manage your apps → Upload an app.
  • For an organization: the Teams admin publishes it from the Teams admin center.

In api0, the Test button checks the chain. Then message the bot: on the first message, it sends the person a link to link their account. Once linked, every action is taken with their identity.

Software vendors: one bot per customer

If you sell software to several companies, the cleanest model is one api0 tenant per customer:

  • each customer has its own tools, users, credits and log;
  • its bot lives in its Azure tenant (Single Tenant), which its security team prefers;
  • you bill usage customer by customer.

You can do the setup for them (with an Azure account in their Microsoft tenant) or send them the steps above: about half an hour on their side.

What your customer gets

  • Your product in the tool they already have open all day.
  • Answers and actions in plain language, no training needed.
  • Every action with the person's own permissions, nothing more.
  • A log of every call.

What you get

  • No bot to write, host or maintain.
  • The same setup serves Claude, WhatsApp and Telegram.
  • A concrete answer to your customers' "AI" requests.

Common problems

Symptom Likely cause
"Invalid App ID" in api0 The secret was pasted into the App ID field. The App ID is a GUID.
Microsoft rejects the App ID / secret pair Expired secret, or wrong Microsoft tenant ID.
The bot doesn't answer Messaging endpoint not pasted in Azure, or Teams channel not enabled.
The app doesn't show up in Teams Custom app upload is disabled: go through the Teams admin.

excerpt: Tes clients vivent dans Microsoft Teams. Voici comment y mettre ton produit — en conversation, avec les droits de chaque utilisateur — sans écrire, héberger ni maintenir un bot.
contentHtml:
Quand un client B2B demande « vous avez quelque chose dans Teams ? », la réponse honnête est souvent non. Parce qu'un bot Teams, ce n'est pas un petit projet :

  • une ressource Azure Bot, une inscription d'app, des secrets qui expirent ;
  • un service web qui reçoit les messages du Bot Framework et y répond ;
  • un moteur de conversation qui comprend les demandes et appelle ton API ;
  • l'authentification de chaque utilisateur, pour qu'il n'agisse qu'avec ses droits ;
  • un manifest d'app Teams, des icônes, une validation par l'admin du client ;
  • et la maintenance de tout ça.

Avec api0, tu gardes la seule partie que Microsoft impose — la ressource Azure Bot — et le reste est fourni.

Comment ça marche

Utilisateur Teams ──► Azure Bot (le tien) ──► api0 ──► ton API
                                               │
                                     outils, identité, journal, crédits
  1. L'utilisateur écrit au bot dans une conversation privée Teams.
  2. Microsoft transmet le message au messaging endpoint fourni par api0.
  3. L'assistant d'api0 comprend la demande et appelle les outils créés à partir de ton API — au nom de cet utilisateur.
  4. La réponse revient dans Teams.

Ce sont les mêmes outils que dans Claude ou WhatsApp : tu configures ton API une seule fois.

Avant de commencer

  • Ton API importée dans api0 (onglet Tools) — voir le guide principal.
  • L'accès réglé (onglet Access) : idéalement, l'identifiant de chaque personne, pour que ton application applique ses propres droits.
  • Un accès au portail Azure avec le droit de créer une ressource Azure Bot.
  • Côté client : un admin Teams qui autorise l'app, ou le chargement d'apps personnalisées autorisé.

Étape 1 — Créer la ressource Azure Bot

  1. Portail Azure → Créer une ressource → Azure Bot.
  2. Nom du bot, abonnement, groupe de ressources. Plan tarifaire : F0.
  3. Type d'app : Single Tenant. Note l'App ID (un GUID) et l'ID du tenant Microsoft.
  4. Dans la ressource → Configuration → Manage Password → New client secret. Copie la valeur immédiatement : Azure ne la montre qu'une fois.

Étape 2 — L'enregistrer dans api0

app.api0.ai → Channels → Teams :

  • App ID, secret, ID du tenant Microsoft ;
  • nom du bot (celui que verront tes utilisateurs) ;
  • optionnel : un prompt système (ton, longueur des réponses, confirmations).

api0 demande immédiatement un jeton à Microsoft avec ces valeurs. Si l'App ID et le secret ne vont pas ensemble, tu le sais tout de suite, avec un message clair — pas trois jours plus tard en production.

En retour, api0 affiche le messaging endpoint de ton bot.

Étape 3 — Brancher Azure sur api0

Dans la ressource Azure Bot :

  1. Configuration → Messaging endpoint → colle l'URL fournie par api0 → Appliquer.
  2. Channels → Microsoft Teams → accepte les conditions → Appliquer.

Étape 4 — Le package d'app Teams

Un bot n'atteint personne tant qu'une app Teams qui le référence n'est pas installée. Cette app est un zip : un manifest.json et deux icônes. C'est souvent là que les projets s'arrêtent.

Dans Channels → Teams, api0 génère le package à partir de ce qu'il sait déjà : App ID, nom du bot, page « Get started » de ton tenant. Tu le télécharges, c'est tout.

L'app est en scope personnel : le bot répond en conversation privée, là où il a du sens.

Tu préfères le préparer toi-même (icônes à ta marque, textes) ? Un template de manifest est fourni.

Étape 5 — Installer et tester

  • Pour toi : Teams → Apps → Gérer vos apps → Charger une app.
  • Pour une organisation : l'admin Teams la publie depuis le Teams admin center.

Dans api0, le bouton Test vérifie la chaîne. Écris ensuite au bot : au premier message, il envoie à la personne un lien pour relier son compte. Une fois relié, chaque action est faite avec son identité.

Éditeur de logiciels : un bot par client

Si tu vends un logiciel à plusieurs entreprises, le modèle le plus propre est un tenant api0 par client :

  • chaque client a ses outils, ses utilisateurs, ses crédits et son journal ;
  • son bot vit dans son tenant Azure (Single Tenant), ce que ses équipes sécurité préfèrent ;
  • tu factures l'usage client par client.

Tu peux faire la mise en place pour lui (avec un compte Azure de son tenant Microsoft) ou lui envoyer la procédure ci-dessus : c'est une demi-heure côté client.

Ce que ton client y gagne

  • Ton produit dans l'outil qu'il ouvre déjà toute la journée.
  • Des réponses et des actions en langage naturel, sans formation.
  • Chaque action avec les droits de la personne, rien de plus.
  • Un journal de chaque appel.

Ce que tu y gagnes

  • Pas de bot à écrire, héberger ou maintenir.
  • La même configuration sert Claude, WhatsApp et Telegram.
  • Un argument de vente concret face aux demandes « IA » de tes clients.

Problèmes fréquents

Microsoft refuse le couple App ID / secret Secret expiré, ou mauvais ID de tenant Microsoft.
Le bot ne répond pas Messaging endpoint non collé dans Azure, ou canal Teams non activé.

title: Connect Your Internal Systems to Claude, Securely
excerpt: Claude Enterprise is rolled out, but it doesn't know your ERP, your CRM or your HR tools. Here's how to open them to Claude without exposing secrets, with each employee's own permissions and a log of every call.
contentHtml:
You've rolled out Claude across the company. Teams use it to write, summarize, analyze. But as soon as a question touches company data — "where is order 4512?", "how many days off do I have left?", "open a ticket for the login bug" — Claude can't do anything. People copy and paste from their tools.

The technical answer exists: the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Claude connects to MCP servers that give it tools. The problem is everything needed around them for security to say yes.

What your security team will ask

  1. Who is acting? Each call must be made as the employee, with their permissions — not with an all-powerful service account.
  2. Where are the secrets? Your systems' credentials must never pass through the AI.
  3. What was done? You need a log: who, which tool, when.
  4. Who can sign in? Employees, through the company identity provider. Not anyone with a link.
  5. Who uses what? Usage must be measurable per team.

Writing an MCP server that ticks these five boxes, for every system, is an infrastructure project. api0 is that layer, ready-made, in front of your existing APIs.

The architecture

Employee in Claude
   │  OAuth 2.1 (PKCE) — sign-in via Entra ID / OIDC
   ▼
api0 (MCP gateway)
   │  checks identity · picks the credential · logs · meters
   ▼
Your internal APIs (ERP, CRM, HR, Azure DevOps…)

Claude only talks to api0. api0 talks to your systems, with the credential you chose.

Step 1 — Connect your identity provider

In the Access tab, set your tenant's sign-in to your OIDC provider: Entra ID, Okta, Google Workspace or another. You need an issuer, a client ID and a secret, created in your IdP for api0.

Result: when an employee adds the connector in Claude, they sign in with their usual company account (MFA, conditional access and the rest included). The IdP client secret is stored encrypted.

Step 2 — Import your internal APIs

Tools tab: import each system's OpenAPI spec, or describe the endpoints in plain English. Each operation becomes a tool, tested before it's enabled.

Import only what's useful. A tool you don't import doesn't exist for Claude. Start with reads (look up an order, a balance, a ticket), add writes later.

Your APIs must be reachable by api0. If they're internal, put a gateway in front that only accepts calls signed by api0 (see step 3).

Step 3 — Choose how api0 authenticates to your systems

This is the decision that matters most.

Best: each employee's identity. Two ways:

  • Their own account, via OAuth: the employee connects their account in the target system once; api0 keeps and refreshes the token.
  • Their own token (an Azure DevOps PAT, for example): the employee adds it once; it's encrypted and can't be read back, only replaced.

Either way, the target system sees the employee, applies their permissions, and attributes the action to them (the author of an Azure DevOps work item really is the person who asked). An employee who hasn't linked their account yet gets a message explaining how — never a call made as someone else.

For your own services: the identity token signed by api0. Your application verifies a Google identity token signed by api0, whose audience names your tenant. No secret to store on your side, and no other api0 customer can produce a token valid for you.

Last resort: a shared credential (fixed token, headers, OAuth client credentials). Simple, but every action is taken by the same account. Keep it for reading non-sensitive data.

Step 4 — Protect personal data

By default, api0 can pass the user's email and tenant ID to your services (X-User-Email, X-Tenant-Id). Useful for your own applications; turn it off for any tool pointed at a third party: your employees' emails then stay inside the platform.

Step 5 — Roll out in Claude

  1. Channels tab → MCP: server URL and Client ID.
  2. Add the connector in Claude (Settings → Connectors). On Claude Enterprise, an admin can make it available to the whole organization.
  3. Create a Claude Project per team, with domain instructions: vocabulary, confirmation rules, answer format. A template is provided.

You can also write tenant instructions in api0 (up to 2,000 characters) that Claude receives on every connection: the main project, naming conventions, what to always check.

Step 6 — Track usage

  • Log (Activity tab): every call, the tool, the person, the result, the latency.
  • Credits: every successful call is metered; a failed call is never billed. You choose whether the tenant pays or each person on their own plan.

The security checklist

Requirement api0's answer
Employee sign-in OAuth 2.1 with PKCE, through your IdP (Entra ID / OIDC)
Actions as the employee Per-person credential (OAuth or personal token)
Secrets kept out of the AI Stored in api0, encrypted (AES-256-GCM), never returned to Claude
Least privilege Only imported operations exist; the target system applies its permissions
Personal data Identity forwarding can be turned off per tool
Traceability A log of every call
Implementation Gateway and store written in Rust

Where to start

One system, one team, two weeks:

  1. Days 1–3: import one internal API, Entra ID sign-in, per-person credentials.
  2. Days 4–5: Claude connector and Project for a pilot team.
  3. Days 6–12: real use, add tools as requests come in.
  4. Days 13–14: review with the usage log.

Next: read the detailed architecture.

contentHtml:
Tu as déployé Claude dans l'entreprise. Les équipes l'utilisent pour écrire, résumer, analyser. Mais dès qu'une question touche aux données de l'entreprise — « où en est la commande 4512 ? », « combien de jours de congé me reste-t-il ? », « crée un ticket pour le bug de connexion » — Claude ne peut rien faire. Les gens copient-collent depuis leurs outils.

La réponse technique existe : le Model Context Protocol (MCP). Claude se connecte à des serveurs MCP qui lui donnent des outils. Le problème, c'est tout ce qu'il faut autour pour que la sécurité dise oui.

Ce que ta sécurité va demander

  1. Qui agit ? Chaque appel doit se faire au nom de l'employé, avec ses droits — pas avec un compte de service tout-puissant.
  2. Où sont les secrets ? Les identifiants de tes systèmes ne doivent jamais transiter par l'IA.
  3. Qu'est-ce qui a été fait ? Il faut un journal : qui, quel outil, quand.
  4. Qui peut se connecter ? Les employés, via le fournisseur d'identité de l'entreprise. Pas n'importe qui avec un lien.
  5. Qui consomme quoi ? L'usage doit être mesurable par équipe.

Écrire un serveur MCP qui coche ces cinq cases, pour chaque système, c'est un projet d'infrastructure. api0 est cette couche, toute faite, devant tes APIs existantes.

L'architecture

Employé dans Claude
   │  OAuth 2.1 (PKCE) — connexion via Entra ID / OIDC
   ▼
api0 (passerelle MCP)
   │  vérifie l'identité · choisit l'identifiant · journalise · décompte
   ▼
Tes APIs internes (ERP, CRM, RH, Azure DevOps…)

Claude ne parle qu'à api0. api0 parle à tes systèmes, avec l'identifiant que tu as choisi.

Étape 1 — Brancher ton fournisseur d'identité

Dans l'onglet Access, configure la connexion de ton tenant avec ton fournisseur OIDC : Entra ID, Okta, Google Workspace ou autre. Il te faut un émetteur (issuer), un client ID et un secret, créés dans ton IdP pour api0.

Effet : quand un employé ajoute le connecteur dans Claude, il se connecte avec son compte d'entreprise habituel (MFA, accès conditionnel et tout le reste compris). Le secret client de l'IdP est stocké chiffré.

Étape 2 — Importer tes APIs internes

Onglet Tools : importe la spec OpenAPI de chaque système, ou décris les endpoints en langage naturel. Chaque opération devient un outil, testé avant d'être activé.

N'importe que ce qui est utile. Un outil non importé n'existe pas pour Claude. Commence par la lecture (consulter une commande, un solde, un ticket), ajoute l'écriture ensuite.

Tes APIs doivent être joignables par api0. Si elles sont internes, place devant elles une passerelle qui n'accepte que les appels signés par api0 (voir étape 3).

Étape 3 — Choisir comment api0 s'authentifie auprès de tes systèmes

C'est la décision qui compte le plus.

L'idéal : l'identité de chaque employé. Deux façons :

  • Son propre compte, en OAuth : l'employé connecte une fois son compte du système cible ; api0 garde et rafraîchit le jeton.
  • Son propre jeton (par exemple un PAT Azure DevOps) : l'employé l'ajoute une fois ; il est chiffré et ne peut plus être relu, seulement remplacé.

Dans les deux cas, le système cible voit l'employé, applique ses droits, et attribue l'action à lui (l'auteur d'un work item Azure DevOps est bien la personne qui a demandé). Un employé qui n'a pas encore relié son compte reçoit un message qui explique comment — jamais un appel fait au nom de quelqu'un d'autre.

Pour tes propres services : le jeton d'identité signé par api0. Ton application vérifie un jeton Google signé par api0, dont l'audience désigne ton tenant. Aucun secret à stocker de ton côté, et un autre client d'api0 ne peut pas produire un jeton valable pour toi.

En dernier recours : un identifiant partagé (jeton fixe, en-têtes, OAuth client credentials). Simple, mais toutes les actions sont faites par le même compte. À réserver à la lecture de données non sensibles.

Étape 4 — Protéger les données personnelles

Par défaut, api0 peut transmettre à tes services l'email de l'utilisateur et l'identifiant du tenant (X-User-Email, X-Tenant-Id). Utile pour tes propres applications, à désactiver pour tout outil pointé vers un tiers : les emails de tes employés restent alors dans la plateforme.

Étape 5 — Déployer dans Claude

  1. Onglet Channels → MCP : URL du serveur et Client ID.
  2. Ajoute le connecteur dans Claude (Paramètres → Connecteurs). Sur Claude Enterprise, un admin peut le rendre disponible pour toute l'organisation.
  3. Crée un Projet Claude par équipe, avec des instructions métier : vocabulaire, règles de confirmation, format des réponses. Un template est fourni.

Tu peux aussi écrire, dans api0, des instructions du tenant (jusqu'à 2 000 caractères) que Claude reçoit à chaque connexion : le projet principal, les conventions de nommage, ce qu'il faut toujours vérifier.

Étape 6 — Suivre l'usage

  • Journal (onglet Activity) : chaque appel, l'outil, la personne, le résultat, la latence.
  • Crédits : chaque appel réussi est décompté ; un appel en échec n'est jamais facturé. Tu choisis si c'est le tenant qui paie ou chaque personne avec son plan.

La checklist sécurité

Exigence Réponse api0
Connexion des employés OAuth 2.1 avec PKCE, via ton IdP (Entra ID / OIDC)
Actions au nom de l'employé Identifiant par personne (OAuth ou jeton personnel)
Secrets hors de l'IA Stockés dans api0, chiffrés (AES-256-GCM), jamais renvoyés à Claude
Moindre privilège Seules les opérations importées existent ; le système cible applique ses droits
Données personnelles Transmission de l'identité désactivable par outil
Traçabilité Journal de chaque appel
Implémentation Passerelle et stockage écrits en Rust

Par où commencer

Un système, une équipe, deux semaines :

  1. Jours 1–3 : import d'une API interne, connexion Entra ID, identifiants par personne.
  2. Jours 4–5 : connecteur Claude et Projet pour une équipe pilote.
  3. Jours 6–12 : usage réel, ajout d'outils selon les demandes.
  4. Jours 13–14 : bilan avec le journal d'usage.

Pour aller plus loin : lis l'architecture détaillée.

title: api0 Architecture and Supported Authentication Models
excerpt: The technical guide: how a request travels through api0, from Claude, Teams or WhatsApp to your application, and every inbound and outbound authentication model, with when to choose which.
contentHtml:
This guide is for technical and security teams evaluating api0. It describes the path of a request, then the two authentication questions every AI gateway has to answer: who is calling, and which credential your application is called with.

Overview

 Claude · Cursor · MCP clients          Teams · WhatsApp · Telegram
            │ MCP (HTTP)                          │ webhooks
            │                                     ▼
            │                          messaging bridge + assistant
            ▼                                     │
   ┌────────────────────── api0 gateway ────────────────────┐
   │ 1. authenticates the caller    4. injects the credential│
   │ 2. resolves tenant and tool 5. calls the application     │
   │ 3. checks credits              6. logs and meters       │
   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
            │                                     │
         store (Postgres)                   your application
   tools · tenants · encrypted secrets   (or a third-party API)

Three components, written in Rust:

  • The gateway receives every call, authenticates it, routes it and logs it. It's the only path to your systems.
  • The store holds the tool registry, tenants, credentials (encrypted) and the usage ledger.
  • The messaging bridge receives webhooks from Teams, WhatsApp and Telegram and runs the assistant, which calls the same tools through the gateway.

The MCP gateway

/mcp is a standard Model Context Protocol server over HTTP (Streamable HTTP). Nothing proprietary at the protocol level: any MCP client works.

Method Behaviour
initialize Negotiates the protocol version, advertises tools, returns the tenant's instructions
tools/list The caller's tenant's tools, and only those
tools/call Routes to the application, meters, returns the result
ping Empty result

Supported protocol versions: 2025-06-18, 2025-03-26, 2024-11-05.

Tenant instructions. initialize returns a text (4,000 characters max) that the client places in front of the model: shared usage rules (load a tool before calling it, take IDs from a listing tool rather than guessing…), the tenant's own text (2,000 characters max) and, for each tool group, its starting tools.

Errors. A refusal from your application comes back as a result flagged isError, with your application's own message: the model reads it and can correct. JSON-RPC errors are reserved for api0's own refusals (unknown tool, invalid parameters, no credits). A failed call is never billed.

What a tool is

A tool is an entry in the registry, scoped to one tenant:

Field Role
name, description, input schema What the model sees
application URL Target, with {parameters} substituted
HTTP verb Set → REST call. Empty → the application speaks MCP natively
content type, body template For APIs whose body isn't the arguments object (JSON Patch…)
static headers The tool's own constants
identity forwarding Whether to send the user's email and tenant
cost, timeout Metering and patience

Importing an OpenAPI spec creates these entries automatically. Body templates cover the hard cases without code: an optional field that wasn't supplied disappears from the body (a whole JSON Patch operation in an array, a single key in an object). Parameter names MCP clients reject ($filter, page[size]) are exposed under a safe name and sent to the application under their real name.

Header order

Applied in this order, last wins:

  1. api0 identity (X-User-Email, X-Tenant-Id) — only if identity forwarding is on;
  2. the tool's static headers;
  3. outbound authentication — always wins a name collision;
  4. Content-Type.

The gateway never sends an internal secret to an application.

Inbound authentication: who is calling?

Model Used by Detail
OAuth 2.1 + PKCE Claude and MCP clients The client registers with the tenant's Client ID; the user signs in; the gateway issues a token bound to that user and that tenant
Google sign-in Default For the dashboard and user sign-in
Your identity provider (OIDC) Enterprises Entra ID or any OIDC IdP configured per tenant: your employees sign in with their account, MFA and conditional access included. The IdP client secret is encrypted
API key Server-to-server integrations One key per tenant or per consumer
Messaging account linking Teams, WhatsApp, Telegram On the first message, the user gets a short-lived link to tie their messaging identity to their account

Acting for an end user

An application can call the gateway with its key on behalf of one of its users, by naming them. The gateway checks this is allowed before any call: the key's owner, always; a consumer key, never for anyone else; a tenant key, only for someone who joined that tenant themselves (through OAuth consent or their own key). Being added as a member is not enough. Otherwise: 403.

Outbound authentication: which credential calls your application?

Each tenant has a default connection, and can add named ones when some tools target a service that needs a different sign-in.

Mode What the application receives When to choose it
none Nothing Public API
api0 identity token (google_sa, no key) A Google identity token signed by api0's service account Your own applications. No secret to store
google_sa with your key An identity token signed by your service account Google Cloud applications (Cloud Run…) with your own IAM
static_bearer Authorization: Bearer <token> Third-party API with a single key
header_injection The headers you define APIs with proprietary headers
client_credentials A token obtained via OAuth client credentials APIs that issue service tokens
per_user — personal secret Each user's own credential: Basic (Azure DevOps PAT), Bearer, or a raw header Per-person attribution and permissions
per_user — OAuth Each user's OAuth token, refreshed by api0 Systems with OAuth sign-in (e.g. Microsoft)

The api0 identity token in detail

For an application you run, the simplest option is often to store no secret at all: the gateway signs every call with api0's service account.

One signer for every tenant means the audience is what separates them, and the tenant doesn't choose it. The gateway builds it from the application URL's origin and the calling tenant's ID:

https://api.example.com/orders  →  aud = https://api.example.com/api0/tenant/<tenant id>

Only the origin is kept: no path or query can spell out another tenant's audience. Your application checks two values, once:

Check Value
aud https://<your origin>/api0/tenant/<your tenant>
email (signer) api0's service account

Pinning the signer is mandatory: any Google service account can mint a token for any audience.

Per-person credentials

This is the model to prefer whenever attribution matters.

  • Personal secret. The user adds their token once (an Azure DevOps PAT, for example). It's encrypted and can't be read back, only replaced. An optional verification URL can check who the token belongs to.
  • OAuth. The user connects their account once. api0 keeps the refresh token encrypted and renews access. The OAuth flow's state value is single-use and short-lived (CSRF protection).
  • No credential yet: the user gets a tool result explaining how to add one. Never a call made as someone else.

Result: the target system sees the real person, applies their permissions and attributes the action to them.

Protecting secrets

  • AES-256-GCM encryption, sealed to the tenant and the secret's purpose: a secret copied into another context won't open.
  • Secrets are never returned to the MCP client, the model or the dashboard (metadata only).
  • With no encryption key configured, the store refuses to save a credential rather than keep it in plain text.

Personal data

Identity forwarding (X-User-Email, X-Tenant-Id) is a per-tool setting. It says who the call is for, not that it came from api0: an application that needs to know that verifies the outbound credential (the signed token). Turn it off for any tool pointed at a third party: your users' emails stay inside the platform.

Usage, credits and logs

  • Every call is logged: tool, user, tenant, status, latency.
  • Every successful call uses credits; a failure is never billed.
  • Billing mode per tenant: the tenant pays, or each person pays on their own plan.

Choosing a model: the decision tree

  1. Is the application yours? → api0 identity token. Nothing to store.
  2. Must actions be attributed to the person, or their permissions applied? → per_user (OAuth if the system supports it, otherwise a personal secret).
  3. Third-party API with a service key? → static_bearer, header_injection or client_credentials, with identity forwarding off.
  4. Tools targeting different services? → one named connection per service.

title: Architecture et modèles d'authentification supportés par api0
excerpt: Le guide technique : comment une requête traverse api0, de Claude, Teams ou WhatsApp jusqu'à ton application, et chaque modèle d'authentification en entrée et en sortie, avec quand choisir lequel.
contentHtml:
Ce guide s'adresse aux équipes techniques et sécurité qui évaluent api0. Il décrit le chemin d'une requête, puis les deux questions d'authentification que toute passerelle d'IA doit résoudre : qui appelle, et avec quel identifiant on appelle ton application.

Vue d'ensemble

 Claude · Cursor · clients MCP          Teams · WhatsApp · Telegram
            │ MCP (HTTP)                          │ webhooks
            │                                     ▼
            │                          pont de messagerie + assistant
            ▼                                     │
   ┌──────────────────── passerelle api0 ───────────────────┐
   │ 1. authentifie l'appelant      4. injecte l'identifiant │
   │ 2. résout le tenant et l'outil  5. appelle l'application    │
   │ 3. vérifie les crédits         6. journalise, décompte  │
   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
            │                                     │
         store (Postgres)                   ton application
   outils · tenants · secrets chiffrés      (ou API tierce)

Trois composants, écrits en Rust :

  • La passerelle reçoit chaque appel, l'authentifie, le route et le journalise. C'est le seul point de passage vers tes systèmes.
  • Le store garde le registre des outils, les tenants, les identifiants (chiffrés) et le registre d'usage.
  • Le pont de messagerie reçoit les webhooks de Teams, WhatsApp et Telegram et fait tourner l'assistant, qui appelle les mêmes outils via la passerelle.

La passerelle MCP

/mcp est un serveur Model Context Protocol standard sur HTTP (Streamable HTTP). Rien de propriétaire côté protocole : tout client MCP fonctionne.

Méthode Comportement
initialize Négocie la version du protocole, annonce les outils, renvoie les instructions du tenant
tools/list Les outils du tenant de l'appelant, et seulement eux
tools/call Route vers l'application, décompte, renvoie le résultat
ping Réponse vide

Versions du protocole acceptées : 2025-06-18, 2025-03-26, 2024-11-05.

Instructions du tenant. initialize renvoie un texte (4 000 caractères max) que le client place devant le modèle : des règles d'usage communes (charger un outil avant de l'appeler, prendre les identifiants dans un outil de listing plutôt que de les deviner…), le texte propre au tenant (2 000 caractères max) et, pour chaque groupe d'outils, les outils de départ.

Erreurs. Un refus de ton application revient comme un résultat marqué isError, avec le message de ton application : le modèle le lit et peut corriger. Les erreurs JSON-RPC sont réservées aux refus d'api0 (outil inconnu, paramètres invalides, crédits épuisés). Un appel en échec n'est jamais facturé.

Ce qu'est un outil

Un outil est une entrée du registre, rattachée à un tenant :

Champ Rôle
nom, description, schéma d'entrée Ce que le modèle voit
URL de l'application Cible, avec des {paramètres} substitués
verbe HTTP Défini → appel REST. Vide → l'application parle MCP nativement
content-type, modèle de corps Pour les APIs dont le corps n'est pas l'objet d'arguments (JSON Patch…)
en-têtes fixes Constantes propres à l'outil
transmission d'identité Envoyer ou non l'email et le tenant de l'utilisateur
coût, timeout Décompte et patience

Importer une spec OpenAPI crée ces entrées automatiquement. Les modèles de corps couvrent les cas difficiles sans code : un champ optionnel non fourni disparaît du corps (une opération JSON Patch entière dans un tableau, une seule clé dans un objet). Les noms de paramètres que les clients MCP refusent ($filter, page[size]) sont exposés sous un nom sûr et renvoyés à l'application sous leur vrai nom.

Ordre des en-têtes

Appliqués dans cet ordre, le dernier gagne :

  1. identité api0 (X-User-Email, X-Tenant-Id) — seulement si la transmission d'identité est activée ;
  2. en-têtes fixes de l'outil ;
  3. authentification sortante — gagne toujours en cas de collision ;
  4. Content-Type.

La passerelle n'envoie jamais de secret interne à une application.

Authentification entrante : qui appelle ?

Modèle Utilisé par Détail
OAuth 2.1 + PKCE Claude et les clients MCP Le client s'enregistre avec le Client ID du tenant ; l'utilisateur se connecte ; la passerelle émet un jeton lié à cet utilisateur et à ce tenant
Connexion Google Par défaut Pour le tableau de bord et la connexion des utilisateurs
Ton fournisseur d'identité (OIDC) Entreprises Entra ID ou tout IdP OIDC configuré par tenant : tes employés se connectent avec leur compte, MFA et accès conditionnel compris. Le secret client de l'IdP est chiffré
Clé API Intégrations serveur à serveur Une clé par tenant ou par consommateur
Liaison de compte messagerie Teams, WhatsApp, Telegram Au premier message, l'utilisateur reçoit un lien de courte durée pour relier son identifiant de messagerie à son compte

Agir pour un utilisateur final

Une application peut appeler la passerelle avec sa clé pour le compte d'un de ses utilisateurs, en le nommant. La passerelle vérifie avant tout appel que c'est permis : le propriétaire de la clé, toujours ; une clé de consommateur, jamais pour quelqu'un d'autre ; une clé du tenant, seulement pour une personne qui a elle-même rejoint ce tenant (par le consentement OAuth ou sa propre clé). Être ajouté comme membre ne suffit pas. Sinon : 403.

Authentification sortante : avec quel identifiant appeler ton application ?

Chaque tenant a une connexion par défaut, et peut en ajouter d'autres, nommées, quand certains outils visent un service qui demande une autre authentification.

Mode Ce que reçoit l'application Quand le choisir
none Rien API publique
Jeton d'identité api0 (google_sa, sans clé) Un jeton d'identité Google signé par le compte de service d'api0 Tes propres applications. Aucun secret à stocker
google_sa avec ta clé Un jeton d'identité signé par ton compte de service Applications Google Cloud (Cloud Run…) avec ton propre IAM
static_bearer Authorization: Bearer <jeton> API tierce à clé unique
header_injection Les en-têtes que tu définis APIs à en-têtes propriétaires
client_credentials Un jeton obtenu par OAuth client credentials APIs qui délivrent des jetons de service
per_user — secret personnel L'identifiant de chaque utilisateur : Basic (PAT Azure DevOps), Bearer, ou en-tête brut Attribution et droits par personne
per_user — OAuth Le jeton OAuth de chaque utilisateur, rafraîchi par api0 Systèmes à connexion OAuth (ex. Microsoft)

Le jeton d'identité api0 en détail

Pour une application que tu opères, le plus simple est souvent de ne stocker aucun secret : la passerelle signe chaque appel avec le compte de service d'api0.

Un seul signataire pour tous les tenants : c'est donc l'audience qui les sépare, et le tenant ne la choisit pas. La passerelle la construit à partir de l'origine de l'URL de l'application et de l'identifiant du tenant appelant :

https://api.exemple.com/orders  →  aud = https://api.exemple.com/api0/tenant/<id du tenant>

Seule l'origine est gardée : aucun chemin, aucune requête ne peut fabriquer l'audience d'un autre tenant. Ton application vérifie deux valeurs, une fois pour toutes :

Vérification Valeur
aud https://<ton origine>/api0/tenant/<ton tenant>
email (signataire) le compte de service d'api0

Épingler le signataire est obligatoire : n'importe quel compte de service Google peut émettre un jeton pour n'importe quelle audience.

Identifiants par personne

C'est le modèle à préférer dès que l'attribution compte.

  • Secret personnel. L'utilisateur ajoute une fois son jeton (par exemple un PAT Azure DevOps). Il est chiffré et ne peut plus être relu, seulement remplacé. Une URL de vérification optionnelle permet de contrôler à qui appartient le jeton.
  • OAuth. L'utilisateur connecte une fois son compte. api0 garde le jeton de rafraîchissement chiffré et renouvelle l'accès. Le paramètre state du flux OAuth est à usage unique et court (protection CSRF).
  • Sans identifiant : l'utilisateur reçoit un résultat d'outil qui lui explique comment l'ajouter. Jamais d'appel fait au nom de quelqu'un d'autre.

Résultat : le système cible voit la vraie personne, applique ses droits et lui attribue l'action.

Protection des secrets

  • Chiffrement AES-256-GCM, scellé selon le tenant et l'usage du secret : un secret copié vers un autre contexte ne s'ouvre pas.
  • Les secrets ne sont jamais renvoyés au client MCP, ni au modèle, ni au tableau de bord (lecture des métadonnées seulement).
  • Sans clé de chiffrement configurée, le store refuse d'enregistrer un identifiant plutôt que de le garder en clair.

Données personnelles

La transmission de l'identité (X-User-Email, X-Tenant-Id) est un réglage par outil. Elle dit pour qui est l'appel, pas qu'il vient d'api0 : une application qui doit le savoir vérifie l'identifiant sortant (le jeton signé). Désactive-la pour tout outil pointé vers un tiers : les emails de tes utilisateurs restent dans la plateforme.

Usage, crédits et journal

  • Chaque appel est journalisé : outil, utilisateur, tenant, statut, latence.
  • Chaque appel réussi décompte des crédits ; un échec n'est jamais facturé.
  • Mode de facturation par tenant : le tenant paie, ou chaque personne paie avec son plan.

Choisir son modèle : l'arbre de décision

  1. L'application est à toi ? → jeton d'identité api0. Rien à stocker.
  2. Les actions doivent être attribuées à la personne, ou ses droits appliqués ? → per_user (OAuth si le système le permet, sinon secret personnel).
  3. API tierce avec une clé de service ? → static_bearer, header_injection ou client_credentials, et transmission d'identité désactivée.
  4. Des outils visent des services différents ? → une connexion nommée par service.

title: Azure DevOps in Claude and Teams, Each Person With Their Own Microsoft Account
excerpt: The step-by-step setup for connecting Azure DevOps to api0 with each person's own Microsoft (Entra ID) sign-in: the organization, the Entra app, admin consent, the api0 wizard and the Connect button, with the errors you'll hit along the way and how to fix them.
contentHtml:
By the end of this guide, you ask Claude or Teams to "create a bug 'Login fails on Safari' and assign it to me", and the work item shows up in Azure DevOps under your name, with your permissions. Nobody pastes a token: each person clicks Connect once and signs in with their Microsoft account. After that, api0 renews access on its own.

Allow an hour for Azure DevOps and another for Teams, errors included.

Throughout the guide, replace:

Placeholder What it is Where to find it
<tenant-id> Your Microsoft directory (Entra ID) ID Entra admin center → Overview → Tenant ID
<organization> Your Azure DevOps organization name dev.azure.com/<organization>
<project> A project in that organization dev.azure.com/<organization>/<project>
<client-id> The ID of the Entra app created in step 2 The app's Overview page

The systems involved

api0 sits in the middle: it never holds anyone's Microsoft password, only each person's token, which Entra ID issues. Every piece carries its address; dotted lines are only used during setup.

The run, step by step

Once per person, Connect:

Then on every request in Teams:

  • 1–3. Connect sends the person to Microsoft: login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant-id>/oauth2/v2.0/authorize. If it breaks: section 5.
  • 4. They sign in with their work account and accept: login.microsoftonline.com. If it breaks: consent, section 3.
  • 5. Entra ID returns a code to api0: gateway.api0.ai/oauth/downstream/callback. If it breaks: the redirect URI, section 2.
  • 6–7. The gateway trades the code and keeps the tokens sealed: login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant-id>/oauth2/v2.0/token. If it breaks: the app's secret, section 2.
  • 8–9. Teams hands the message to the Bot Framework, which posts it, signed, to api0's messaging endpoint: smba.trafficmanager.net. If it breaks: the messaging endpoint, section 6.4.
  • 10. api0 checks the message really comes from Microsoft: login.botframework.com. If it breaks: the Azure Bot, section 6.2.
  • 11. The model picks the tool, for the linked person. If it breaks: link your Teams account, section 6.6.
  • 12–13. The person's token is renewed if it expired, without asking: login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant-id>/oauth2/v2.0/token. If it breaks: press Connect again.
  • 14–15. Azure DevOps creates the work item with that token, so in their name and with their rights: dev.azure.com/<organization>/<project>/_apis/wit/workitems. If it breaks: project access, section 1.
  • 16–18. The reply goes back to Teams with the bot's token: smba.trafficmanager.net. If it breaks: the Azure Bot, section 6.2.

From Claude, steps 8 to 11 become one call from Claude to gateway.api0.ai/mcp, the result of step 15 goes back to Claude, and steps 16 to 18 don't happen.

Domains

Domain System Role in the flow
app.api0.ai api0 dashboard Setup wizard, Channels, Settings → My access tokens (Connect). The settings page is app.api0.ai/?view=settings.
gateway.api0.ai api0 gateway Receives every call, picks the person's token, calls Azure DevOps
gateway.api0.ai/mcp api0 gateway The connector URL you add in Claude
gateway.api0.ai/oauth/downstream/callback api0 gateway Where Microsoft sends people back after Connect. Registered in the Entra app.
gateway.api0.ai/oauth/idp/callback api0 gateway Where Microsoft sends people back after signing in to api0, if you chose Microsoft sign-in
Teams messaging endpoint (shown in Channels → Microsoft Teams) api0 gateway Where the Azure Bot delivers Teams messages
api0.ai api0 website Privacy policy and terms the Teams app links to
login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant-id> Entra ID Sign-in and consent page; issues and renews each person's token
entra.microsoft.com Entra admin center App registration, consent, users, roles, sign-in logs
portal.azure.com Azure portal The Azure Bot
admin.microsoft.com Microsoft 365 admin center Teams licence: trial, assignment, billing
admin.teams.microsoft.com Teams admin center Approving the Teams app, custom-app policies
teams.microsoft.com Microsoft Teams Where people chat with the bot
dev.azure.com/<organization> Azure DevOps Where the work items live
aex.dev.azure.com Azure DevOps account page Creating the organization on the right directory

Accounts

You need three kinds of account. Keep them apart.

Account Example Role
api0 account owner@gmail.com Owns the api0 tenant and signs in to app.api0.ai. Can be any email: it's not your Microsoft identity.
Directory administrator you_domain#EXT#@<directory>.onmicrosoft.com (a personal Microsoft account added to the directory) Creates the Entra app, grants consent, creates users, assigns licences. Never use it for Connect: see section 5.
Work account demo@<directory>.onmicrosoft.com What people use for Connect, Teams and Azure DevOps. A plain user: a Teams licence, Basic access in Azure DevOps, and no admin role.

What a new, non-admin person does

A new colleague with a plain work account:

  1. Their administrator adds them to Azure DevOps (Basic, project group Contributors) and gives them a Teams licence.
  2. They open https://dev.azure.com/<organization> once in a browser, so Azure DevOps knows them.
  3. They sign in to app.api0.ai (or follow the tenant's Get started page), then Settings → My access tokens → Connect, with their work account.
  4. In Teams, they open the bot, link their account with the code from api0 (section 6.6), and ask.

They can only do what their own Azure DevOps permissions allow. What they create is attributed to them, never to someone else. Without project access, Azure DevOps refuses, and api0 grants nothing on top.

1. An Azure DevOps organization on the right directory

The organization must be connected to the same Entra directory as the app you'll create in step 2. That directory is the one that issues the tokens.

  1. Open a private window and go to https://aex.dev.azure.com/me.
  2. Sign in with an account from that directory (ideally the one that administers it).
  3. In the directory drop-down, pick the one whose ID is <tenant-id>.
  4. Create new organization, then a project. Choose the Agile process if you want a Bug type: the Basic process only has Epic, Issue, Task and Test Case, so there you ask for an Issue.
  5. Check in Organization settings → Microsoft Entra that the directory shown is yours.

Error TF400813: The user is not authorized to access this resource. The user is not a member of the AAD directory that the target Organization is connected to. The browser was signed in with another account (a personal one, or one from another directory), and Azure DevOps picked the wrong directory. The private window and explicitly choosing the directory on aex.dev.azure.com/me fix it.

2. An Entra app dedicated to api0

Create an app just for api0. Don't reuse an existing one (another product's app, or one that accepts personal Microsoft accounts): Azure services only accept work accounts, and you want to be able to revoke api0 without breaking anything else.

In Entra admin center → Identity → Applications → App registrations → New registration:

  • Name: api0 downstream
  • Supported account types: Accounts in any organizational directory (multitenant). Not personal accounts. "Multitenant" lets a customer later consent to the same app in their own directory.
  • Redirect URI: Web platform, https://gateway.api0.ai/oauth/downstream/callback

If people will also sign in to api0 with their Microsoft account (option Microsoft 365 (Entra ID) in step 4), the same app can do it: in Authentication, add a second Web redirect URI, https://gateway.api0.ai/oauth/idp/callback. One app, two redirect URIs, one secret.

Then, in the app:

  1. Certificates & secrets (left menu, Manage section) → Client secrets tab → New client secret. Copy the Value column right away, not the Secret ID: it won't be shown again. Keep it for step 4 and don't send it to anyone. If it ever ends up in a chat, an email or a screenshot, delete it and create a new one.
  2. API permissions → Add a permission, as Delegated:
    • Azure DevOps → user_impersonation
    • Azure Service Management → user_impersonation, only if you also want tools that read your Azure subscription (resources, costs).

Can't find "Certificates & secrets"? You're probably in Certificate authorities, a directory-wide security setting. The secret is created inside the app: open App registrations → All applications → api0 downstream, and the menu appears on the left.

3. Admin consent

Still in API permissions, click Grant admin consent for <your directory>. The permissions should turn green, Granted.

Error Could not grant admin consent. Your organization does not have a subscription (or service principal) for the following API(s): … A directory created for something else (licensing, for instance) may not have the local entry (the service principal) for Microsoft's services. Create them with Azure CLI:

az login --tenant <tenant-id> --allow-no-subscriptions

az ad sp create --id 499b84ac-1321-427f-aa17-267ca6975798

That's Azure DevOps, usually the one missing. If the message also listed Microsoft Graph (00000003-0000-0000-c000-000000000000) or Azure Service Management (797f4846-ba00-4fd7-ba43-dac1f8f63013), run the same command with their ID. A reply of "The service principal name … is already in use" means it already exists: nothing to do. Then click Grant admin consent again.

4. The api0 wizard

Which api0 account?

Today an api0 account owns a single tenant, and the wizard replaces that tenant's default connection. If your account already serves another integration, create a second api0 account (another email address) for this one.

Your api0 account's email has nothing to do with the Microsoft account: at Connect, Microsoft asks you to sign in, and you pick the account from your directory. An api0 account on Gmail that connects to Azure DevOps as firstname@your-company.com works fine.

Coming soon: named connections will allow several connections in one tenant, for example Azure DevOps as the default plus an arm connection for Azure Resource Manager, without a second account.

The screens

On app.api0.ai, start the setup wizard (offered at first sign-in, or through your tenant's Reconfigure button):

  1. Where do your people's work accounts live?: Microsoft 365 (Entra ID). People then sign in to api0 as themselves, which needs the second redirect URI from step 2.
  2. Import your API: download the Azure DevOps endpoints, replace every YOUR-ORGANIZATION in the file with <organization>, and upload it. It lands as an API named Azure DevOps, under Custom API Groups on the API page, where you can edit it like any other API. Its tools reach Claude as azure-devops-create-work-item, azure-devops-query-work-items and so on. Importing another file later keeps it, unless that file has an API with the same name.
  3. Whose account should the API see?: Each person connects their own account.
  4. Your application in Entra ID:
Field Value
Entra directory (tenant) ID <tenant-id>
Application (client) ID <client-id>, a GUID like c481c32b-…
Client secret the Value copied in step 2
Scope 499b84ac-1321-427f-aa17-267ca6975798/user_impersonation offline_access

Two things to watch:

  • Client ID and Client secret are easy to swap. The client ID is always a GUID (xxxxxxxx-xxxx-…). A secret looks like ofk8Q~…. If you paste the secret into the Client ID field, Microsoft answers AADSTS700016 at Connect.
  • The scope isn't optional for Microsoft. The field's grey text is an example, not a value. An empty scope gives AADSTS900144. 499b84ac-… is Azure DevOps.

Prefer api0 accounts for signing in? On screen 1 choose Neither. On screen 3 choose Someone else's service, then Other options and Each person connects their own account. Screen 4 then also asks for the authorization endpoint https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant-id>/oauth2/v2.0/authorize and the token endpoint https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant-id>/oauth2/v2.0/token. The scope must then include offline_access as shown above.

Reconfiguring later. Your tenant's Reconfigure button reopens this wizard with the saved values filled in. Secrets are never shown back: paste a new one, or leave the field empty if it says it's saved, and the stored one is kept.

  1. The last screen tests the connection with a read-only call. It should fail with a message along the lines of "you haven't added your access yet": expected, since you haven't connected your account. The configuration is already saved. A Connect your account button sits right under the message: it does the same thing as step 5 below.

5. Connect

In Settings → My access tokens, your tenant shows Not connected and a Connect button:

  1. Click Connect.
  2. Microsoft asks you to sign in: pick your account from the <tenant-id> directory.
  3. You land back on api0 with Your account is connected.

Once connected, the button becomes Reconnect: use it to sign in again, or to switch to another work account. The settings page is also reachable directly at app.api0.ai/?view=settings.

Never connect with an account that holds an admin role. On a directory with Security defaults (on by default in new directories), administrators must use multi-factor sign-in. api0 renews tokens in the background, where nobody can answer a multi-factor prompt, so Microsoft refuses the renewal. In our test, the work account was given Billing, License and Teams Administrator after it connected. The next morning:

  • the Entra sign-in log (Monitoring & health → Sign-in logs → User sign-ins (non-interactive)) showed the attempt for the app as Interrupted;
  • api0's gateway logged invalid_grant;
  • the bot answered that access wasn't set up.

Fix: remove the admin roles, then Reconnect. Do the administration with a separate account.

api0 now enforces this. Connect refuses an account that holds any directory role beyond an ordinary user's, and says so on My access tokens. If an account becomes an admin after connecting, the bot says so at the next renewal instead of "access not set up". The same happens when Microsoft demands a multi-factor sign-in.

The account must have opened Azure DevOps once. Azure DevOps refuses API calls from an account that has never signed in to its website. The check then answers HTTP 403, and the reply's title says "Identity … has not been materialized, please use interactive login over the browser first". Open https://dev.azure.com/<organization> once in a browser with that account, then run the check again. Each new person in the tenant needs to do this once too.

Still the same 403 after opening Azure DevOps? Check for a personal account. If your directory was created from a personal Microsoft account (common for a subscription opened for something else), that account sits in the directory as an external member. In Entra admin center → Users, its user principal name looks like firstname_domain#EXT#@<directory>.onmicrosoft.com. Connect gets a token for that directory identity, while dev.azure.com signs you in as the personal account itself, so Azure DevOps never meets the identity in the token. To find out, search for the ID quoted in the error under Users. The fix is a native work account:

  1. Entra admin center → Users → New user → Create new user, for example demo@<directory>.onmicrosoft.com.
  2. Azure DevOps → Organization settings → Users → Add users: that account, access level Basic, project <project>, group Project Contributors.
  3. In a private window, open https://dev.azure.com/<organization>/<project> as that account and set its password.
  4. In api0, Connect again. On Microsoft's account picker, choose Use another account and sign in with the work account.

In a real company, people already have work accounts, and this doesn't come up.

If Microsoft shows an error page, come back to api0 with reload, not just the browser's Back button: a page restored by Back may keep its buttons greyed out.

Every person in the tenant does the same, once. They act only with their own Azure DevOps permissions, and nothing is ever attributed to someone else.

6. In Teams

Teams reaches api0 through an Azure Bot of your own, in your directory. New bots are single-tenant: the people chatting with it must be in the same directory as the bot. Each person still connects their own Azure DevOps account (step 5); Teams only carries the conversation.

6.1 A Teams licence in your directory

Teams is a Microsoft 365 licence on the directory, not part of an Azure subscription. To check, sign in at https://teams.microsoft.com with a work account from <tenant-id>. "You don't have the required permissions to access this org" means no licence.

For a demo, use a Microsoft Teams Essentials trial, from inside your directory:

  1. Give the account that will buy it the Billing Administrator role (Entra admin center → Users → the user → Assigned roles). The self-service sign-up page refuses an account your organisation manages, with "ask your administrator": buy from the admin center instead.
  2. admin.microsoft.com → Billing → Purchase services → Microsoft Teams Essentials → Start free trial.
  3. Licences are assigned in the Microsoft 365 admin center only (Entra now refuses). That needs the License Administrator role.
  4. Set the user's Usage location first (Entra → Users → the user → Edit properties → Settings), or the assignment fails with "invalid usage location".
  5. Billing → Licenses → Microsoft Teams Essentials → Assign licenses → the user.
  6. Billing → Your products: turn Recurring billing off if it's offered.

Wait about ten minutes, then check that https://teams.microsoft.com opens.

In a company that already has Teams, skip all of this.

6.2 The Azure Bot

In https://portal.azure.com, Create → Azure Bot:

Field Value
Bot handle any name, e.g. api0-demo-bot
Resource group a new one, e.g. api0-demo
Data residency Global
Pricing tier Change plan → Free (F0)
Type of App Single Tenant
Creation type Create new Microsoft App ID

Then, in the bot → Configuration: copy the Microsoft App ID and the App Tenant ID. Click Manage Password → New client secret and copy its Value.

6.3 Connect the bot in api0

On app.api0.ai → Channels → Microsoft Teams, paste the App ID, the Microsoft tenant ID and the secret, and set a Bot name. That name is what everyone sees in Teams; left empty, it's the tenant name. Click Connect: api0 asks Microsoft for a token before saving, so a typo shows up here.

6.4 Point the bot at api0

  1. In the Microsoft Teams block on api0's Channels page, the box Finish in Azure and Teams shows the Messaging endpoint. Copy it.
  2. In Azure, bot → Configuration → Messaging endpoint: paste it, Apply.
  3. Bot → Channels → Microsoft Teams: accept the terms, Apply. It should show as running.

The same api0 block also offers to link your Teams account right away. Wait until the app is installed (6.5): before that, the bot can't receive the code.

6.5 Install and approve the app

  1. In the same Finish in Azure and Teams box, click Download Teams app. Keep the .zip as it is.
  2. In Teams, Apps → Manage your apps → Upload an app. If your directory doesn't allow personal uploads, Teams submits the app to your organisation instead, and it shows as Pending.
  3. A Teams Administrator approves it in https://admin.teams.microsoft.com → Teams apps → Manage apps → the app:
    • Publish the submitted version;
    • set Status to Allowed (a newly submitted app is Blocked);
    • Actions → Org-wide app settings → Custom apps → Let users interact with custom apps: on.

On a directory where Teams was just added, the admin center first shows "We're setting up your new app management experience", and Publish stays grey for up to 30 minutes. Wait, then reload.

Approved changes can take up to an hour to reach Teams. The app then appears under Apps → Built for your org.

If Publish stays grey for hours, install the app for yourself instead: in the Teams admin center, Teams apps → Setup policies → Global (Org-wide default) → Upload custom apps: On, and keep custom apps allowed org-wide. About 15 minutes later, in Teams: Apps (the ⊞ icon in the left bar) → Manage your apps → Upload an app → Upload a custom app.

Renaming later (or getting api0's logo on an app downloaded before it had it):

  1. api0 takes the Bot name only when connecting. On Channels → Microsoft Teams, click Disconnect, then fill in the form again: the same App ID and Microsoft tenant ID, the secret, and the new Bot name, e.g. api0. Linked accounts and the Messaging endpoint stay as they were. If you didn't keep the secret's Value, create a new one first (bot → Configuration → Manage Password → New client secret).
  2. Click Download Teams app again. Each download carries a higher version number, which Teams requires for an update.
  3. In https://admin.teams.microsoft.com → Teams apps → Manage apps, open the app, click Upload file and choose the new .zip. Don't add it as a new app: it has the same ID.
  4. Publish it if the admin center asks.

Teams takes the name and the icon from this app, not from the Azure Bot: its Bot profile in Azure can stay as it is. The new name can take up to an hour to reach Teams.

6.6 Link your Teams account and try it

  1. In api0, Channels → Microsoft Teams → Link your own Teams account. A short code appears. It is single-use and expires after a few minutes; open the box again for a new one.
  2. In Teams, click Chat and find the bot by its name. If it's not in the list, start a new chat and type its name.
  3. Paste the code in the message box and send it. The bot answers: "Linked. You are now <api0 email> here."
  4. Ask it something real, for example:
    Create an issue "Login fails on Safari" in project <project> and assign it to firstname@<directory>.onmicrosoft.com
  5. Open https://dev.azure.com/<organization>/<project>/_workitems/recent: the work item is there, Created By your work account.

Name the assignee with the work email. The bot knows you by your api0 email, which Azure DevOps doesn't know, so it can't work out "me".

If the bot says the type doesn't exist, your project uses the Basic process: ask for an Issue instead of a Bug.

Roles in a test directory. Above, the test account was given Billing Administrator, License Administrator and Teams Administrator to do all of this. In a real company, an existing administrator does these steps. In a test directory, remove those roles afterwards.

Error recap

Message Cause Fix
TF400813 … not a member of the AAD directory Wrong account or directory in the browser Private window, aex.dev.azure.com/me, pick the directory
No "Certificates & secrets" You're in Certificate authorities Open the app itself under App registrations
Could not grant admin consent … no service principal The directory lacks the local entry for a Microsoft service az ad sp create --id <service ID>, then consent again
… is already in use when creating a service principal It already exists Nothing to do
The wizard's final test fails You haven't clicked Connect yet Connect your account, or Settings → My access tokens → Connect
AADSTS700016: Application with identifier '…' was not found The Client ID field holds something else, often the secret Client ID = the app's GUID; create a new secret if the old one was exposed
AADSTS900144: The request body must contain the following parameter: 'scope' Empty scope 499b84ac-1321-427f-aa17-267ca6975798/user_impersonation offline_access
AADSTS50011 (redirect URI mismatch) The app lacks the api0 redirect URI Add …/oauth/downstream/callback (and …/oauth/idp/callback for Microsoft sign-in) as Web
HTTP 403, Identity … has not been materialized, please use interactive login over the browser first The account has never opened Azure DevOps in a browser Open dev.azure.com/<organization> once with that account, then check again
The same 403, even after opening Azure DevOps The token is for a personal account's #EXT# identity in the directory Create a native work account, add it to the organization, Connect with it
Teams: You don't have the required permissions to access this org No Teams licence in the directory 6.1: Teams Essentials trial
Teams Essentials sign-up: "ask your administrator" Self-service sign-up refuses managed accounts Buy from admin.microsoft.com → Billing → Purchase services
You don't have access to assign licenses Billing Administrator can buy, not assign Add License Administrator
License assignment cannot be done for user with invalid usage location The user has no country Entra → the user → Edit properties → Settings → Usage location
Entra: licence changes "only available within the M365 Admin Center" Entra no longer assigns licences admin.microsoft.com → Billing → Licenses
Teams app Pending after upload Personal uploads not allowed, so the app was submitted to the organisation Teams admin center → Manage apps → Publish
Publish greyed out, "setting up your new app management experience" Teams admin center being prepared for the directory Wait up to 30 minutes
Teams app Blocked Default for a newly submitted app Status → Allowed; allow custom apps org-wide
Wizard buttons greyed out after coming back from Microsoft Page restored by the browser's Back Reload the page
Bot: access "not set up, or has expired" the day after Connect; gateway log invalid_grant; Entra sign-in log Interrupted The connected account holds an admin role and must use multi-factor sign-in, which a background renewal can't do Remove the admin roles, then Reconnect
Work item type Bug does not exist in project The project uses the Basic process Ask for an Issue, or use an Agile project
